## Swarm Mode

You are now in "agent swarm" mode. The user may send tasks that require a large number of parallel subagents.

## Workflow

You do not need to use TodoList to record this workflow.

1. First, you may need to do a small amount of exploratory work before deciding how to divide the task across subagents. You may not need subagents during this exploratory phase.

2. After exploring, if you are convinced no subagent is needed to complete the task, tell the user why and wait for further instructions; otherwise, continue with the appropriate delegation.

3. Once you have enough context, do not handle the main work yourself. Use AgentSwarm with a `prompt_template` containing the `{{item}}` placeholder and an `items` array for the requested or appropriate number of subagents, partitioning the problem so each item gives one subagent a distinct part of the work. Pass `subagent_type` when the whole swarm should use a non-default subagent profile.

## Coordination

- Give each subagent a distinct scope of work.
- Avoid duplicating work across subagents.
- Avoid assigning conflicting changes or responsibilities to different subagents.
- Remember that subagents have your full capabilities. Do not overload their prompts with excessive detail; only describe the necessary background and each subagent's specific task.
- Unless the user explicitly specifies a lower limit, do not try to conserve the number of agents. AgentSwarm supports up to 128 subagents and queues launches automatically, so decompose work as finely as possible while keeping subagent responsibilities non-conflicting; combine tasks only when they are genuinely inseparable. If the subagents only need to read, inspect, or report back without making changes, their scopes may overlap slightly.
</system-reminder>

.. _algorithm:

The jusText algorithm
=====================

jusText is a heuristic-based tool for removing boilerplate content (such as
navigation links, headers, footers and advertisements) from HTML pages and
keeping only the main content (full text). The algorithm works in three
stages:

1. **Segmentation into paragraphs** — the HTML document is converted to a DOM
   and traversed with a SAX parser. Whenever a block-level element (``p``,
   ``div``, ``td``, ``h1`` .. ``h6``, ``li``, ``pre``, ...) is encountered,
   the text collected so far is closed off as a new *paragraph*. A paragraph
   is a coherent block of text that appears between block-level tags.

2. **Context-free classification** — each paragraph is classified, in
   isolation, into one of four classes: *good*, *bad*, *short* or *neargood*.

3. **Context-sensitive re-classification** — the intermediate classes
   (*short* and *neargood*) are resolved into *good* or *bad* by looking at
   the classification of the surrounding paragraphs.

After re-classification, the paragraphs marked as *good* constitute the main
content of the page; the paragraphs marked as *bad* are boilerplate and are
discarded.

Context-free classification
---------------------------

Each paragraph is evaluated on its own, using the following criteria:

* **Link density** — the ratio of characters inside links to the total number
  of characters in the paragraph. If the link density exceeds
  ``max_link_density`` (default ``0.2``), the paragraph is classified as
  **bad**. Navigation menus and link lists are caught by this rule.

* **Stopwords density** — the ratio of stopwords (frequent, content-free
  words from a language-specific stoplist, e.g. "the", "a", "of" in English)
  to all words in the paragraph. Real, grammatical text contains many
  stopwords, while boilerplate (menus, button labels, copyright notices)
  contains few. This is the key signal that makes jusText
  language-aware but free of any linguistic processing beyond a word list.

* **Length** — the number of characters in the paragraph.

A paragraph is classified as follows:

* If the link density is higher than ``max_link_density``, the paragraph is
  **bad**.
* Otherwise, if the paragraph is longer than ``length_high`` (default 200
  characters) **and** its stopwords density is at least ``stopwords_high``
  (default ``0.32``), the paragraph is **good** — it is long and reads like
  real text.
* Otherwise, if the paragraph is longer than ``length_low`` (default 70
  characters) **and** its stopwords density is at least ``stopwords_low``
  (default ``0.30``), the paragraph is **neargood** — it looks promising but
  does not quite meet the full criteria.
* Otherwise, if the paragraph contains no words at all, it is **bad**
  (empty or blank paragraphs carry no content).
* Otherwise, the paragraph is **short** — too short to decide on its own.

In addition, two hard rules mark a paragraph as **bad** regardless of the
measurements above:

* any paragraph containing the copyright symbol ``©`` (typically a copyright
  notice in the footer), and
* any paragraph containing a ``<select>`` element (typically a language or
  site switcher, not real content).

Context-sensitive re-classification
-----------------------------------

The *short* and *neargood* classes are only temporary. They are resolved in
the second pass, which looks at each such paragraph's nearest neighbouring
paragraphs whose class is already decided (*good* or *bad*):

* A **short** paragraph is reclassified based on its nearest neighbours with
  a decided class. If the nearest good/bad neighbour on both sides (before
  and after) is *bad*, the paragraph becomes **bad**; a short paragraph
  surrounded by or adjacent to *good* content becomes **good**.
* A **neargood** paragraph becomes **bad** only when **both** of its nearest
  classified neighbours are *bad*; otherwise it becomes **good**.

The idea is that boilerplate tends to come in clusters (a menu is many short
link paragraphs in a row), while the main content forms long runs of good
paragraphs. A borderline paragraph inside a good run is likely content; one
surrounded by boilerplate is likely boilerplate itself.

Headings
--------

Headings (text in ``h1`` .. ``h6`` tags) are treated specially. They are
usually short, so the context-free pass classifies them as *short*. To keep
the titles of the main content, a heading is reclassified (promoted) to
**good** when it appears within ``max_heading_distance`` characters (default
200) before a *good* paragraph. This behaviour can be turned off with the
``no_headings`` option, in which case all headings are kept *bad*.

.. _algorithm:

The jusText algorithm
=====================

jusText is a heuristic-based tool for removing boilerplate content (such as
navigation links, headers, footers and advertisements) from HTML pages and
keeping only the main content (full text). The algorithm works in three
stages:

1. **Segmentation into paragraphs** — the HTML document is converted to a DOM
   and traversed with a SAX parser. Whenever a block-level element (``p``,
   ``div``, ``td``, ``h1`` .. ``h6``, ``li``, ``pre``, ...) is encountered,
   the text collected so far is closed off as a new *paragraph*. A paragraph
   is a coherent block of text that appears between block-level tags.

2. **Context-free classification** — each paragraph is classified, in
   isolation, into one of four classes: *good*, *bad*, *short* or *neargood*.

3. **Context-sensitive re-classification** — the intermediate classes
   (*short* and *neargood*) are resolved into *good* or *bad* by looking at
   the classification of the surrounding paragraphs.

After re-classification, the paragraphs marked as *good* constitute the main
content of the page; the paragraphs marked as *bad* are boilerplate and are
discarded.

Context-free classification
---------------------------

Each paragraph is evaluated on its own, using the following criteria:

* **Link density** — the ratio of characters inside links to the total number
  of characters in the paragraph. If the link density exceeds
  ``max_link_density`` (default ``0.2``), the paragraph is classified as
  **bad**. Navigation menus and link lists are caught by this rule.

* **Stopwords density** — the ratio of stopwords (frequent, content-free
  words from a language-specific stoplist, e.g. "the", "a", "of" in English)
  to all words in the paragraph. Real, grammatical text contains many
  stopwords, while boilerplate (menus, button labels, copyright notices)
  contains few. This is the key signal that makes jusText
  language-aware but free of any linguistic processing beyond a word list.

* **Length** — the number of characters in the paragraph.

A paragraph is classified as follows:

* If the link density is higher than ``max_link_density``, the paragraph is
  **bad**.
* Otherwise, if the paragraph is longer than ``length_high`` (default 200
  characters) **and** its stopwords density is at least ``stopwords_high``
  (default ``0.32``), the paragraph is **good** — it is long and reads like
  real text.
* Otherwise, if the paragraph is longer than ``length_low`` (default 70
  characters) **and** its stopwords density is at least ``stopwords_low``
  (default ``0.30``), the paragraph is **neargood** — it looks promising but
  does not quite meet the full criteria.
* Otherwise, if the paragraph contains no words at all, it is **bad**
  (empty or blank paragraphs carry no content).
* Otherwise, the paragraph is **short** — too short to decide on its own.

In addition, two hard rules mark a paragraph as **bad** regardless of the
measurements above:

* any paragraph containing the copyright symbol ``©`` (typically a copyright
  notice in the footer), and
* any paragraph containing a ``<select>`` element (typically a language or
  site switcher, not real content).

Context-sensitive re-classification
-----------------------------------

The *short* and *neargood* classes are only temporary. They are resolved in
the second pass, which looks at each such paragraph's nearest neighbouring
paragraphs whose class is already decided (*good* or *bad*):

* A **short** paragraph is reclassified based on its nearest neighbours with
  a decided class. If the nearest good/bad neighbour on both sides (before
  and after) is *bad*, the paragraph becomes **bad**; a short paragraph
  surrounded by or adjacent to *good* content becomes **good**.
* A **neargood** paragraph becomes **bad** only when **both** of its nearest
  classified neighbours are *bad*; otherwise it becomes **good**.

The idea is that boilerplate tends to come in clusters (a menu is many short
link paragraphs in a row), while the main content forms long runs of good
paragraphs. A borderline paragraph inside a good run is likely content; one
surrounded by boilerplate is likely boilerplate itself.

Headings
--------

Headings (text in ``h1`` .. ``h6`` tags) are treated specially. They are
usually short, so the context-free pass classifies them as *short*. To keep
the titles of the main content, a heading is reclassified (promoted) to
**good** when it appears within ``max_heading_distance`` characters (default
200) before a *good* paragraph. This behaviour can be turned off with the
``no_headings`` option, in which case all headings are kept *bad*.

The following figure illustrates the context-sensitive classification:

.. figure:: cs_classification_example.png
   :alt: Example of the context-sensitive classification
   :align: center

   An example of the context-sensitive classification of paragraphs. Short
   and neargood paragraphs (yellow) are reclassified according to their
   nearest good (green) and bad (red) neighbours.

``length_high``       200       Minimum number of characters for a paragraph to

``stopwords_low``     0.30      Minimum stopwords density for a *neargood*
                                paragraph.
``stopwords_high``    0.32      Minimum stopwords density for a *good*
                                paragraph.
``max_link_density``  0.2       Maximum allowed link density. Paragraphs with a
                                higher link density are *bad*.
``max_heading_dist-   200       Maximum distance (in characters) between a
